column5: Fear of the Lord and despising instruction
column6: The commentary contrasts the one who fears and remembers with the ashqa who avoids reminder; Proverbs makes fear of the Lord the beginning of knowledge and says fools despise wisdom and instruction.

column5: Finding Wisdom and finding life
column6: The commentary sets the one who receives reminder against the one who turns aside; Wisdom says finding her brings life and favor from the Lord.

column5: Harming oneself by hating Wisdom
column6: The commentary says the wretched person makes his own condition by putting the reminder aside; Wisdom says the one who misses her harms himself and those who hate her love death.

column5: Despising a word brings ruin
column6: The commentary links avoiding the offered reminder to the ashqa’s ruin; Proverbs says the person who despises a word will be destroyed, while reverence for the command brings reward.

column5: Israel would not hear the Lord
column6: The commentary says the same reminder is offered but some turn from it; the psalm says God’s people would not listen to his voice or submit to him.

column5: Handed over to one’s own counsel
column6: The commentary treats turning away as the hearer’s own choice; the psalm says God gave the unheeding people over to their stubborn hearts to walk in their own counsels.

column5: Willingness and obedience bring good
column6: The commentary says one person takes the reminder while another rejects it; Isaiah places willingness and obedience opposite rebellion, with the former receiving the land’s good.

column5: Refusal and rebellion bring judgment
column6: The commentary links the ashqa’s avoidance with the consequence of his chosen response; Isaiah says those who refuse and rebel will be devoured by the sword.

column5: Called, but not answered
column6: The commentary emphasizes that the reminder has already come to the hearer; Isaiah says God called and spoke but the people did not answer or hear, instead choosing what displeased him.

column5: The offered path is refused
column6: The commentary contrasts receiving reminder with turning aside; Jeremiah invites the people to stand at the crossroads and ask for the good ancient path, but they answer that they will not walk in it.

column5: The watchmen’s warning is not heard
column6: The commentary separates the messenger’s act of warning from the audience’s response; Jeremiah says watchmen sounded the trumpet, but the people replied that they would not listen.

column5: Rejecting the word of the Lord
column6: The commentary identifies the ashqa by his refusal of reminder; Jeremiah says the wise have rejected the word of the Lord, so their claim to wisdom is exposed.

column5: Circumcising the heart
column6: The commentary reads remembering, avoiding, and purifying as acts done upon oneself; Moses calls Israel to circumcise the heart and stop being stiff-necked, a concrete demand for inward change.

column5: Do not postpone good when it is at hand
column6: The commentary says the reminder is beside the hearer yet treated as a foreign neighbor; Proverbs says not to tell a neighbor to return tomorrow when the needed good is already with you, an ethical parallel to leaving available good within reach unused.

column5: Delighting in Torah day and night
column6: The commentary pictures the reminder as something one may take near and work into oneself; Psalm 1 describes the blessed person delighting in the Lord’s Torah and meditating on it continually.

column5: Two ways with opposed endings
column6: The commentary develops a split between the one who receives reminder and the one who avoids it; Psalm 1 says the Lord knows the righteous way while the wicked way perishes.

column5: Rain watering the earth
column6: The commentary’s lexical aside links the south wind and its clouds with the pasture scene in 87:4; Psalm 65 describes God watering the earth and blessing its growth, a specific rain-provision image beside that reading.

column5: Pastures clothed with flocks
column6: The commentary links its wind-and-cloud aside to the surah’s pasture; Psalm 65 closes with pastures clothed with flocks and valleys covered with grain, a related scene of rain’s result.

column5: A nearby neighbor can be closer than distant kin
column6: The commentary develops the “side” as the place of either companion or stranger and says the reminder remains beside the person; Proverbs values the neighbor who is near over a brother who is far away, giving relational weight to nearness.

column5: Wash and make yourselves clean
column6: The commentary’s triad includes purifying oneself as a deliberate act; Isaiah commands people to wash, make themselves clean, and cease doing evil, a direct ethical image of self-correction.

column5: Clean hands and a pure heart
column6: The commentary says purification is one of the hearer’s own responses; the psalm describes the person fit to approach God as one with clean hands and a pure heart.

column5: Make a new heart and turn from transgression
column6: The commentary links avoiding reminder with a self-made ruin and purification with a chosen response; Ezekiel calls Israel to cast away transgressions and make a new heart and spirit so they may live.

column5: Moses asks Pharaoh to humble himself
column6: The commentary’s Moses asks Pharaoh whether he will purify himself, followed by Pharaoh’s rejection; Exodus has Moses and Aaron ask how long Pharaoh will refuse to humble himself before the Lord, making the refusal to heed a direct point of contact.

column5: Abraham and Balaam as opposed moral types
column6: The commentary presents Abraham as entrusting himself to God and seeking distance from idolatry; Avot contrasts disciples of Abraham, marked by humility and a good eye, with Balaam’s pride and acquisitiveness, giving a Jewish ethical interpretation of the Abrahamic posture.

column5: Prophetic speech that is heard but not understood
column6: The commentary stresses one reminder offered while hearers differ in response; Isaiah’s commission says the people will hear without understanding, framing prophetic speech as a judicial hardening, a different emphasis from the commentary’s open invitation.

column5: Hearing that does not lead to turning
column6: The commentary contrasts the person who receives admonition with the one who avoids it; Isaiah’s commission describes closed eyes and dull hearts so the people do not turn and be healed, a contrary account of how the warning functions.

column5: The broad road leads to destruction
column6: The commentary develops two opposed responses and their outcomes; Jesus describes a broad gate and road leading to destruction, entered by many, as a concrete image of the destructive path.

column5: The narrow way leads to life
column6: The commentary contrasts the ashqa with one who receives reminder; Jesus says the narrow way leads to life and is found by few, giving the other side of the two-path image.

column5: Hearing or rejecting the messenger
column6: The commentary says the messenger offers reminder but does not control its reception; Jesus says whoever hears his messengers hears him and whoever rejects them rejects him.

column5: Do not refuse the one who speaks
column6: The commentary ties turning away from reminder to judgment; Hebrews warns its hearers not to refuse the one speaking, recalling that those who rejected the earthly warning did not escape.

column5: People will not endure sound teaching
column6: The commentary says some turn away from reminder because of their chosen response; Paul warns that people will reject sound teaching and gather teachers to suit their desires.

column5: Turning the ear from truth
column6: The commentary makes turning away the decisive act of the ashqa; Paul says people will turn their ears away from the truth and turn aside to myths.

column5: The Scriptures testify to life
column6: The commentary says reminder is already present and offered; Jesus says the hearers search the Scriptures, which testify about him.

column5: Unwilling to come for life
column6: The commentary says the wretched one keeps the reminder nearby but will not receive it; Jesus tells his hearers they are unwilling to come to him to have life.

column5: People love darkness rather than light
column6: The commentary describes the person who chooses distance from beneficial reminder; John says people loved darkness rather than light because their deeds were evil.

column5: Evil deeds avoid the light
column6: The commentary’s avoider moves away from the reminder; John says the one who does evil hates the light and does not come to it, lest his deeds be exposed.

column5: Doing truth and coming into the light
column6: The commentary contrasts turning away with inward moral change; John says the one who does what is true comes to the light so his deeds may be seen as done in God.

column5: Love of this life risks losing it
column6: The commentary links avoiding reminder to preferring the present worldly life; Jesus says the one who loves his life loses it, while the one who hates his life in this world keeps it for eternal life.

column5: The rejected stone is precious to believers
column6: The commentary says the same reminder is differently received; Peter says the stone rejected by builders is precious to those who believe, giving a Christian image of one message/object valued by some and refused by others.

column5: A stumbling stone for the disobedient
column6: The commentary portrays the ashqa as turning aside from what is offered; Peter says others stumble because they disobey the word, a specific outcome of rejection.

column5: The word rejected by some hearers
column6: The commentary says the reminder’s offer is unchanged but its hearers divide; Paul and Barnabas say their hearers have rejected the word and judged themselves unworthy of eternal life.

column5: Other hearers rejoice and believe
column6: The commentary contrasts the person who turns away with the one who receives reminder; Acts says Gentile hearers rejoice and believe after the same proclamation that some rejected.

column5: Jesus makes Nineveh’s repentance a witness
column6: The commentary treats taking warning as the positive alternative to turning away; Jesus says Nineveh repented at Jonah’s proclamation and will condemn the generation that refuses a greater warning, a Christian rereading of Jonah’s response.

column5: The crowd silences a blind petitioner
column6: The commentary recounts a blind man who comes seeking help while another turns away from him; Mark’s crowd rebukes blind Bartimaeus and tells him to be silent, but he cries out all the more.

column5: The blind petitioner follows the way
column6: The commentary pairs the blind man’s humble approach with the person who avoids admonition; Jesus restores Bartimaeus and he follows Jesus on the road, a distinct reversal in which the blind petitioner responds and follows.

column5: Invited guests make excuses
column6: The commentary says the same reminder is offered but its recipients choose whether to respond; in Jesus’ banquet parable, the invited guests begin making excuses and refuse the invitation.

column5: The blind and poor are brought to the feast
column6: The commentary’s Abasa scene gives attention to a blind seeker whom a prominent person neglects; after the invited guests refuse, the servant brings the poor, crippled, blind, and lame to the banquet.

column5: The blind see and the seeing are judged
column6: The commentary uses the blind visitor to expose the failure of a sighted, socially prominent person to recognize who may benefit; Jesus says he came so that those who do not see may see and those who see may become blind.

column5: Claimed sight leaves guilt intact
column6: The commentary opposes the humble blind seeker to the one who turns away; Jesus tells the Pharisees that their claim to see leaves their sin, unlike the blind man whose encounter leads to sight.

column5: A messenger leaves when a household refuses to hear
column6: The commentary limits the messenger to offering reminder and leaves response with the audience; Jesus tells messengers to leave and shake the dust off when a house or town will not receive or hear them.

column5: Pay attention lest one drift away
column6: The commentary describes the ashqa as moving away from the reminder; Hebrews urges close attention to what has been heard lest hearers drift away from it.

column5: Do not quench the Spirit
column6: The commentary presents refusal as a response that can suppress what is offered; Paul warns the community not to quench the Spirit.

column5: Do not despise prophecies
column6: The commentary says the reminder is offered but may be put aside; Paul tells the community not to despise prophetic utterances, a direct instruction against rejecting admonition.

column5: Work out salvation with fear and trembling
column6: The commentary reads self-purification and receiving reminder as deliberate action, and distinguishes it from the messenger’s work; Paul tells believers to work out their salvation with fear and trembling.

column5: God works in the willing hearer
column6: The commentary says human response remains dependent on God’s willing; Paul immediately says God is at work in believers both to will and to work, adding divine agency to the self-directed effort.

column5: Hearing the voice and opening the door
column6: The commentary says the reminder is beside a person yet may be kept outside; Revelation pictures Christ standing at a door and knocking, with fellowship following if someone hears and opens.

column5: The burdened are invited to rest
column6: The commentary contrasts the easy path prepared for the messenger with the hardship of the one who rejects guidance; Jesus invites the weary and burdened to come to him for rest.

column5: The yoke is easy and the burden light
column6: The commentary connects wretchedness with hardship opposite the easy path; Jesus describes his yoke as easy and his burden as light, offering a contrasting response to a divine invitation.

column5: Torment continues day and night forever
column6: The commentary reads the condemned condition as prolonged, with neither death nor life; Revelation portrays the devil and the beast’s followers as tormented day and night forever, a related image of unending punishment.
